Foundations: what a proposal is and reading the call

You will learn the two main kinds of proposal (grant proposals to funders and business proposals to clients), how a reviewer actually reads one, and how to study a call for proposals before writing a single line. You finish the module with a clear go or no-go decision and a folder of the documents most funders ask for.
Grant proposals and business proposals: who reads them and why

A **proposal** is a written offer that asks a reader to commit something, usually money, to a plan you will carry out. It explains a problem or need, what you will do about it, what it will cost, and how the reader will know it worked. Every proposal is really an answer to one question from the reader: **why should I trust you with this?**
A woman presenting a written plan
A proposal is a plan written down so that someone else can decide to fund it or buy it.
Two families of proposal

In this course you will meet two kinds of proposal. A **grant proposal** goes to a funder such as a foundation, an embassy small-grants fund, a development agency, a company's corporate social responsibility (CSR) programme or a government scheme. The funder does not buy anything for itself. It pays you to create change for other people, for example training women, improving a clinic or supporting farmers. A **business proposal** goes to a client who will pay you for a product or service, for example a school that wants 300 branded exercise books or a shop owner who wants you to manage her social media for three months.

The two families share the same backbone. Both start from the reader's need, describe a clear piece of work, give a price or budget, set a timeline and show why you can be trusted. Once you can write one well, the other becomes much easier.
Solicited and unsolicited

A **solicited** proposal answers an invitation. Funders publish a **call for proposals** (also called a request for proposals or RFP, or a notice of funding opportunity). Clients may send a request for quotation. An **unsolicited** proposal is one you send without being asked, for example to a company whose CSR focus matches your project. Solicited proposals have clearer rules and fairer chances. Unsolicited ones need a very short, sharp first contact, usually a one or two page concept note, because nobody is waiting for them.
The standard sections
Funders use different headings, but most full grant proposals contain these parts. A business proposal uses the same logic with simpler names, shown in brackets.
**Cover letter** and **executive summary**: the whole proposal in one page (client: summary).
**Organisation background**: who you are and what you have done before (client: about us).
**Problem statement** or need: what is wrong, for whom, with evidence (client: your situation).
**Goal and objectives**: the change you aim for, written so it can be measured (client: outcomes).
**Activities and workplan**: what you will do, when and who is responsible (client: scope and timeline).
**Logframe or theory of change**: how activities lead to results.
**Budget and budget notes**: the cost of each item and why it is needed (client: price and payment terms).
**Monitoring and evaluation (M&E)**: how you will track and prove results (client: how we report progress).
**Sustainability and risks**: what continues after the money ends, and what could go wrong.
**Annexes**: registration documents, CVs, letters of support, quotes.
How reviewers read

Most funders score proposals against written **evaluation criteria**, often with points for each section, for example relevance, quality of design, budget and value for money, organisational capacity and sustainability. Reviewers may read dozens of proposals for one call. They skim the summary, check eligibility, then look for the sections that carry points. If an answer is hard to find, they may simply give it fewer points. Your job is to make every scoring point easy to see.
Write for a tired reader

Use the funder's own headings in the same order as the call, short paragraphs, numbers instead of adjectives and one idea per paragraph. A reviewer who finds answers quickly is a reviewer in a good mood.

Worked example: same skill, two proposals
For example, Amaka in Lafia, Nasarawa State, trains women to make soap and liquid detergent. She is preparing two documents in the same month.

Grant proposal: a foundation's small-grants call funds women's economic empowerment. Amaka proposes to train 40 women over 6 months, give each a starter kit and follow them up to measure income. She asks for about ₦4.8 million (illustrative figure).

Business proposal: a private secondary school wants liquid soap for its hostels. Amaka proposes to supply 60 litres per month for one school term at an agreed price per litre, with delivery on the first Monday of each month.
For the grant, the reader cares about results for the 40 women and how money is spent. For the school, the reader cares about quality, price, reliability and payment terms.
The same skill produces two very different documents, because the reader and the question 'why should I trust you?' are different.

Many proposals are rejected before anyone reads the project idea, because the applicant was not eligible, missed a required document or ignored the format. Reading the call carefully is the cheapest way to raise your chances. Plan to read it at least three times: once for understanding, once with a pen to mark every rule, and once against your finished draft.

The words **must**, **shall** and **required** mark rules that can disqualify you. Words like **preferred**, **priority** or **an advantage** mark things that earn extra points. Copy every 'must' into a checklist and treat it as non-negotiable.

Deadlines and time zones

Note the exact closing time and time zone. Many international funders use UTC or their own local time, which may be different from West Africa Time (WAT). Portals often slow down near the deadline, so plan to submit at least one full day early.
Asking clarifying questions

Many calls give an email address or a question period, and some publish all questions with answers for every applicant to see. Ask only what the call does not answer, keep it short, and quote the section you are asking about. For example: 'Section 3.2 lists eligible applicants as registered non-profits. Is a cooperative society registered with the state cooperatives department eligible?' Do not ask the funder to judge your idea in advance, and never try to contact reviewers privately.
The go or no-go decision
Writing a good proposal can take many days. Before you start, score the opportunity honestly. A clear 'no' saves you time for a better call.
Go or no-go questions
We meet every eligibility rule
Our idea fits the priorities
We can meet the deadline
We can deliver and report
Budget fits the funding range
If any answer is a firm no, do not apply to this call, and note it for a future one.
Worked example: Amaka reads a call
For example, Amaka's women's cooperative in Lafia finds an illustrative small-grants call on a funding listing site. She reads it with a pen and a notebook.
Priorities: women's economic empowerment in Nigeria. Her soap and detergent training fits directly.
Eligibility: registered organisations with a bank account in the organisation's name and at least two years of activity. The cooperative is registered and has run savings groups for four years. Pass.
Funding: up to ₦5,000,000 for 6 to 12 months, no vehicles, administration costs capped at a percentage stated in the call. Her plan of about ₦4.8 million for 6 months fits.
Criteria: relevance 25, design 30, budget 20, capacity 15, sustainability 10. She writes these on the top of her notebook page.
Submission: one PDF, 10 pages maximum, budget in the funder's template, two annexes. She enters the deadline in her phone calendar with a reminder 5 days before.
Go or no-go: she answers yes to all five questions.
Decision: GO. Her compliance checklist has 18 rows, and design (30 points) tells her to spend the most effort on objectives, activities and the logframe.

Finally, read any guidance notes, templates and frequently asked questions that come with the call. Funders often hide important rules there, such as which costs are allowed, how to count beneficiaries or what to put in each annex. If the funder gives a budget template or application form, use it exactly as provided; do not redesign it or move its columns.
Where calls are published

Calls appear on funders' own websites, embassy and agency pages, newsletters and listing sites. Always confirm a call on the funder's official website before you spend time on it, because copies on other sites can be out of date.

Write a capacity statement you can defend

Most proposals ask why your organisation can deliver. The strongest answer uses facts that a funder could check: how long you have worked, how many people you have reached, what you delivered for whom, and what systems you use for money and records. Avoid big words like 'world-class' or 'unparalleled'. A reviewer trusts 'we trained 85 women in three savings groups between 2023 and 2025, with attendance records' far more than 'we are leaders in women's empowerment'.
Never overstate

Do not claim partners who have not agreed, numbers you cannot prove, or results you have not measured. Funders check references and visit projects. One false claim can end a relationship with a funder for good, and in a grant agreement it can be treated as misrepresentation.
Spotting fake grant offers

Fraudsters know that women's groups and small businesses are looking for funding. Common tricks include messages saying you have 'won' a grant you never applied for, requests for a 'processing fee', 'registration fee' or 'clearance fee' before money is released, and pressure to act within hours. Real funders do not charge you to receive a grant.

You will write a problem statement backed by evidence, turn it into SMART objectives, plan activities on a workplan, and connect everything with a simple theory of change and logframe. Write a problem statement of 200 to 300 words

The **problem statement** (also called the needs statement or statement of need) tells the reader what is wrong, for whom, and why it matters now. It is the foundation of the whole proposal: your objectives must fix the problem you describe, and your activities must address its causes. A weak problem statement makes every later section look weak.
A person researching with documents and charts
Good problem statements are built from evidence you gathered, not from general feelings.
Four questions a good problem statement answers
**Who** is affected? Be specific: 'women aged 25 to 50 who trade in Lafia's main market', not 'women in Africa'.
**Where and how many?** Name the community, ward or local government area, and give numbers you can support.
**What is the problem and how big is it?** Describe the situation in measurable terms, such as income, attendance, distance or cost.
**Why does it happen?** Name the root causes your project will tackle, so the reader sees why your activities make sense.
Use a problem tree

A **problem tree** is a simple drawing used in project planning. Write the core problem on the trunk. Below it, as roots, write its causes, and ask 'why?' again for each cause until you reach things a project could change. Above it, as branches, write its effects. Your project should work on the roots; the branches show why the problem matters.
Problem tree, from effects down to causes
Effects: school fees unpaid, stress
Core problem: low, unstable income
Cause: no saleable skill
Cause: no starting capital
Root: no training or kits nearby
Read from the top: effects sit on the core problem, which rests on causes your project can change.

Your own data is often the most convincing evidence for a small, local project, because national figures rarely describe your ward. A simple baseline survey of the people you plan to serve gives you numbers no one else has, and it becomes the starting point for measuring results later.
Never invent or round up evidence

Use figures exactly as the source gives them and name the source. If you cannot find a reliable figure, describe what you observed and how, for example 'In our March survey of 40 members, 31 said...'. A made-up statistic is easy for a reviewer to spot and destroys trust in everything else.
Common mistakes
Describing the lack of your solution as the problem: 'the problem is that there is no soap-making centre'. The real problem is low income; a centre is one possible answer.
Writing about the whole country or continent instead of your target group.
Using emotional words with no numbers: 'terrible suffering', 'extreme poverty'.
Listing causes your project will not touch, which makes your activities look too small.
Worked example: Amaka's problem statement
For example, Amaka surveyed 40 members of her cooperative in Lafia in one week, using a one-page paper form and her phone to record answers.
She asked each woman her average monthly profit from trading over the last 3 months, whether she had any production skill, and what stopped her starting a new product.
Results (illustrative): 29 of 40 (73%) earned less than ₦20,000 profit per month; 34 of 40 had no production skill; 26 named lack of training as the main barrier and 22 named starting capital.
She drew a problem tree: core problem 'low and unstable income', causes 'no saleable skill' and 'no money for first materials', effects 'children's fees paid late' and 'no savings'.

She wrote: 'In Lafia main market, most women in our cooperative earn too little to meet household needs. In our survey of 40 members (March), 29 earned under ₦20,000 profit monthly and 34 had no production skill. Members already buy soap and detergent weekly from outside the community, yet none produce them. The main barriers they named were lack of practical training (26 women) and starting capital (22 women)...'
Result: a 240-word problem statement that names the group, gives numbers with their source and points straight to the two causes her project will address: skills and starter capital.

Keep the statement focused on the people you will serve. One or two sentences of wider context, such as a national figure from a named report, can help, but most of the space should describe your target group in your location. End by pointing towards the causes your project will tackle, so the reader moves naturally into your objectives.
Link need to opportunity

A strong statement shows both the problem and the opportunity. Amaka shows that soap is bought every week locally, so a skill in making it has a ready market. Funders like problems that have a practical, local solution.

Once the reader understands the problem, they want to know exactly what change you will create and how. This section has three layers: a broad **goal**, a few measurable **objectives**, and the **activities** that achieve them, shown on a **workplan**.
A person standing beside a target with goals
A goal names the direction; objectives name the measurable change you promise.
Goal and objectives

The **goal** is the long-term change your project contributes to, often bigger than your project alone, for example 'improved household income and financial security for women in Lafia'. **Objectives** are the specific changes your project will achieve and measure within its time and budget. Most small projects have two to four objectives.
Write objectives using **SMART**: Specific (who and what), Measurable (a number), Achievable (realistic with your resources), Relevant (fixes the problem you described) and Time-bound (by when).
Weak objective
Why it is weak
SMART version
Empower women economically
Not specific, not measurable, no time
By month 6, at least 30 of 40 trained women are selling their own soap or detergent at least twice a month
Train many women in soap making
How many? To what standard?
By month 3, 40 women complete 12 days of training and each produces a correctly cured batch under supervision
Increase incomes
By how much, for whom, by when?
By month 6, at least 25 of 40 participants report a monthly profit increase of ₦10,000 or more compared with the baseline
Outputs are not outcomes

'40 women trained' is an output: something you deliver. 'Women selling regularly and earning more' is an outcome: the change that results. Funders want to see both, but objectives should mainly describe outcomes. You will use this distinction again in the logframe.
From objectives to activities

For each objective, list the activities needed to reach it. Each activity should be something a person does, starting with a verb, with a clear owner and a date. Include preparation (recruitment, buying materials), delivery (training, mentoring), and follow-up (data collection, reporting). Reviewers often find gaps here, such as no time for recruitment or no budget line for a key activity.
Write each objective at the top of a page.
Under it, list every activity needed, beginning with a verb: recruit, buy, train, mentor, survey, report.
Assign one responsible person to each activity.
Estimate when each activity starts and ends.
Check that every activity has a matching line in the budget, and every budget line has a matching activity.
The workplan

A **workplan**, often drawn as a **Gantt chart**, shows activities as rows and months as columns, with shaded cells for when each happens. It proves your plan is realistic in time and helps you spot clashes, such as training during a festive season or planting season when participants are busy.
Amaka's six-month workplan
M1: recruit, baseline, buy
M2 to M3: 12 training days
M3: starter kits issued
M4 to M6: mentoring, market days
M6: endline survey, report
Each phase on the timeline matches activities in the plan and lines in the budget.
Worked example: Amaka's objectives and activities
For example, Amaka turns her problem statement into objectives and a plan for 40 women over 6 months.
Goal: improved and more stable household income for women in the cooperative.
Objective 1 (skills): by month 3, 40 women complete 12 days of practical training in safe soap and liquid detergent production and record keeping.
Objective 2 (enterprise): by month 6, at least 30 of the 40 women sell their own products at least twice a month.
Objective 3 (income): by month 6, at least 25 women report a monthly profit increase of ₦10,000 or more compared with the baseline survey.

Activities for Objective 1: recruit 40 women using agreed criteria (month 1, Amaka); hire 2 trainers (month 1, committee chair); deliver 12 training days, 2 per week (months 2 to 3, trainers); issue PPE and keep attendance sheets (months 2 to 3, coordinator).

Activities for Objectives 2 and 3: issue 40 starter kits (month 3); hold monthly mentoring meetings and phone check-ins (months 4 to 6); organise 3 market days (months 4 to 6); run endline survey (month 6).
Result: 3 SMART objectives, 10 activities each with an owner and month, and a 6-month Gantt chart that fits on half a page.

Notice how each objective answers part of the problem statement. Amaka's survey found two barriers, skills and starting capital, so Objective 1 builds skills and the starter kits under Objective 2 address capital. Her income objective uses the same measure as her baseline (monthly profit), so the change can be compared fairly at the end. When a reviewer can trace a straight line from problem to objective to activity, the design score goes up.
Be realistic, not impressive
Promise what you can deliver. Meeting a modest target builds a funder's trust for a bigger second grant. Missing an inflated target damages your record.

Funders want to see the logic of your project: why your activities should lead to the change you promise. Two tools show this. A **theory of change** explains the pathway in words or a diagram. A **logical framework**, or **logframe**, puts the same logic into a table with indicators. Some funders ask for one, some for both, and many small funders accept a simple version.
A person turning an idea into a plan

The results chain

Both tools rest on the same chain. **Inputs** are resources: money, people, materials. **Activities** are what you do with them. **Outputs** are the direct products of activities, fully under your control, such as women trained or kits issued. **Outcomes** are changes in people's behaviour or situation that result, such as women selling and earning more. **Impact** is the long-term change your project contributes to, such as reduced household poverty. The further along the chain, the less control you have, which is why assumptions matter.

Theory of change in plain words

Write your theory of change as a short chain of **if... then...** statements, and add the **assumptions** that must hold true for each link to work. An assumption is a condition outside your direct control. If an assumption is risky, your plan should include something to manage it.
Worked example: Amaka's theory of change
For example, Amaka writes her theory of change in five sentences for her proposal.

IF 40 women receive practical training in safe soap and detergent making plus simple record keeping, THEN they will have the skills to produce good quality products. Assumption: women can attend 2 sessions a week.
IF trained women receive starter kits, THEN they can produce their first batches without borrowing. Assumption: materials stay available at prices close to the budget.
IF they get mentoring and access to market days, THEN they will sell regularly. Assumption: local demand for affordable soap and detergent continues.
IF they sell regularly and track costs, THEN their profit and income will increase. Assumption: prices cover costs; the training teaches costing.
IF incomes rise and remain stable, THEN households will be more financially secure (goal).
Result: a clear chain that a reviewer can follow in one minute, with assumptions that her mentoring and costing training directly address.
The logframe

The classic logframe is a table with four rows and four columns. The rows follow the results chain from top to bottom: Goal, Outcome (sometimes called purpose), Outputs and Activities. The columns are: **narrative summary** (what you aim for), **indicators** (how you measure it), **means of verification** (where the evidence comes from) and **assumptions** (conditions outside your control). Funders' templates vary, so always use theirs if they provide one.

Read a logframe from the bottom up as a chain of 'if and': if activities happen and the assumptions hold, then outputs are delivered; if outputs are delivered and assumptions hold, then the outcome follows, and so on. A common mistake is putting the same thing at two levels, for example 'women trained' as both output and outcome. Ask yourself: is this something we deliver, or a change in people that results? Another mistake is assumptions that are really risks you could manage, such as 'trainers turn up'. That is your job, not an assumption. Reviewers judge value for money, measurability and what lasts after the grant. The budget is the proposal written in numbers. A reviewer uses it to check whether your plan is realistic, whether costs are reasonable for your area, and whether every activity is paid for. A budget that is too high looks wasteful; one that is too low suggests you do not understand the work and may fail to deliver.
An abacus for counting and calculating
Every budget line is a small calculation: quantity times unit cost.
The structure of a line-item budget

Each line shows four things: the **item**, the **unit** (day, month, person, piece), the **quantity** and the **unit cost**. The **total** is quantity multiplied by unit cost. Group lines into categories such as personnel, materials and equipment, venue and logistics, monitoring and evaluation, and administration. Always use the funder's template if it gives one.
Types of cost
**Direct costs**: spent only on this project, such as trainers' fees, materials and venue hire.

**Indirect or administrative costs**: shared running costs of your organisation, such as part of office rent, accounting and internet. Many funders allow these only up to a percentage stated in the call; never exceed it.

**In-kind contributions**: things you or partners provide without asking the funder for money, such as a free hall or volunteer time. Show their estimated value in a separate column; they prove commitment.
**Ineligible costs**: things the funder will not pay for, listed in the call. Common examples are vehicles, land, debts and alcohol. Leave them out completely.

Collecting good data
Use the same questions at baseline and endline, so results can be compared fairly.
Keep simple tools: attendance sheets signed each day, a one-page sales record book for each woman, a short survey form.
Combine numbers with stories: a few short case studies, collected with consent, help explain why results happened.
Protect people's data: store forms safely, share only summary figures, and get permission before using names or photos.
Record problems honestly. Funders value learning; hiding failure is far worse than reporting it.
Evaluation questions funders often use

Many development funders use the OECD DAC evaluation criteria. These ask about **relevance** (does the project meet real needs?), **coherence** (does it fit with other work in the area?), **effectiveness** (did it achieve its objectives?), **efficiency** (were resources used well?), **impact** (what wider difference did it make?) and **sustainability** (will benefits last?). Even if your funder does not name them, answering these questions in your M&E section makes it stronger.

Funders want their money to leave something lasting behind. They also want to see that you have thought about what could go wrong. These two sections are often short and vague in weak proposals, which makes them an easy place to earn points that competitors lose.
A small green seedling growing
Sustainability means the change keeps growing after the grant ends.
Writing about sustainability

Sustainability is not a promise that the project will continue forever. It means explaining which benefits will last after funding ends, and how. Give concrete mechanisms, not hopes. Common types include: **skills** that stay with people, **income** that pays for itself, **local ownership** by a committee or cooperative, **partnerships** with schools or government, and **diversified funding** from other sources.
Worked example: Amaka's sustainability section
For example, Amaka writes 4 short paragraphs, each with a clear mechanism.
Skills: the 40 women keep the skills, safety gear and record books; 6 of the strongest will be trained as peer trainers.
Income: each woman sets aside ₦500 from every ₦5,000 of sales in a materials fund within the cooperative savings group, so she can buy her next batch without a grant.
Market: links with 3 schools and the weekly market create regular buyers beyond the project.
Ownership: the cooperative committee owns the programme, will run a second training paid by members' fees from year 2, and has written this into its annual plan.
Result: a sustainability section that names who will carry on, how it will be paid for, and what is already in place.

Be careful not to promise sustainability you cannot control. 'The state government will take over the programme' is weak unless you have a letter saying so. 'The cooperative will charge members ₦5,000 per place for the second training, as agreed at the general meeting in May' is strong, because it is specific and already decided. Where possible, attach evidence such as meeting minutes or partner letters.

Common reasons proposals fail
**Not eligible or not compliant**: wrong organisation type, missing documents, over the page limit, late submission.
**Poor fit**: a good project sent to a funder with different priorities.
**Vague problem or objectives**: no evidence, no numbers, nothing measurable.
**Broken logic**: activities do not lead to the objectives, or the logframe does not match the narrative.
**Unrealistic budget**: too high or too low, arithmetic errors, ineligible costs, totals that do not match.
**Weak capacity**: no proof the team has delivered similar work or can manage money.
**No sustainability or risk thinking**: nothing explains what happens after the grant.
**Generic writing**: copied text from another proposal, wrong funder name left in, or the call's questions not answered directly.

Notice that most of these reasons have nothing to do with how good the idea is. A strong idea can still be rejected if it is badly presented, sent to the wrong funder or submitted incomplete. The good news is that these are the easiest problems to fix, because a careful process, not talent, prevents them. If a funder sends feedback after a rejection, read it closely and record it in your master file, because the same weaknesses tend to come back.
The copy-and-paste trap
Reusing your master text is smart; sending the wrong funder's name or an old project's figures is fatal. Search the final document for every funder and project name you have used before.

A business proposal asks a client to buy your product or service. The client does not care about your theory of change; they care whether you understood their problem, exactly what they will receive, when, for how much and on what terms. The biggest danger in client work is unclear scope, which leads to disputes, unpaid extra work and lost customers.
Two people completing a signed agreement
A clear client proposal can be signed and used as the agreement itself.
Structure of a business proposal
**Their situation**: restate the client's need in their words, from your conversation.
**Proposed solution**: what you will provide and how it solves the need.
**Scope of work**: deliverables, quantities, standards, what is included and what is not.
**Timeline**: key dates and milestones.
**Price and payment terms**: the cost, how and when it is paid.
**About you**: short credentials, past clients, samples or photos of work.
**Terms and acceptance**: validity period, change rules, how to accept.
Scope: inclusions and exclusions

**Scope creep** happens when a client keeps adding small requests that were never priced. Prevent it by stating exactly what is included, with quantities, and then listing what is **not** included. Exclusions feel awkward to write, but they protect both sides, because the client knows what to expect and you know what you are paid for.
Vague scope versus protective scope
Vague
Protective
Supply liquid soap to the school
Deliver regularly
Good quality product
Price negotiable
60 litres per month, 5-litre jerrycans
Delivered first Monday monthly
Labelled with batch number
₦X per litre, fixed for the term
Protective scope uses numbers, dates and standards so both sides can check delivery.
Worked example: Amaka's school supply proposal
For example, after meeting the bursar of a private secondary school, Amaka writes a 3-page proposal. Prices are illustrative.
Situation: 'The school needs about 60 litres of liquid hand and dish soap each month for 2 hostels and the kitchen, delivered reliably.'

Included: 60 litres per month in 12 sealed 5-litre jerrycans, labelled with product name, batch number and production date; delivery to the school store on the first Monday of each month for one term (3 months); replacement of any faulty batch within 3 working days.
Not included: dispensers, deliveries outside the agreed date, quantities above 60 litres (available at the same unit price with 5 days' notice), cleaning services.
Price: ₦1,500 per litre x 60 litres = ₦90,000 per month; ₦270,000 for the term.
Payment terms: 50% (₦45,000) on acceptance before the first delivery, then the balance of each month's supply within 7 days of delivery, by bank transfer to the business account.
Validity and acceptance: price valid for 30 days from the proposal date; accepted when the bursar signs and returns the acceptance page.
Result: the school knows exactly what it gets and pays; Amaka knows that a request for dispensers or extra deliveries is a new, separately priced order.

Look at how the proposal starts with the client's situation, not with Amaka's story. The bursar reads her own problem first, in words from their meeting, and immediately sees that Amaka listened. Credentials come later and stay short: how long she has produced soap, two or three current customers who agreed to be named, and a photo of the labelled jerrycans. A client buys confidence that the work will be done right, and specific scope does more for that confidence than a long description of your business.
Presenting price and terms
Show the calculation (quantity x unit price) so the client can see how you arrived at the total.
Say whether prices include delivery, VAT or other charges, if these apply to your business.
Give payment terms in plain numbers: amount, date and method. A deposit protects you when you must buy materials first.
State how long the price is valid, because your costs can change.
Offer options only if they help the client decide, for example a basic and a premium package. Three options at most.
Payment safety

Ask clients to pay only into your business account, and confirm transfers in your banking app before delivering, not from a screenshot or SMS alert, which can be faked. Send payment details in the signed proposal so nobody can later claim different account details.

Before you set a price, know your own costs. Add up materials, packaging, transport and your time for the quantity in the proposal, then add your profit margin. If the client pushes for a lower price, reduce the scope (for example fewer litres or less frequent delivery) rather than cutting your margin to nothing. A proposal that wins work at a loss is not a success.
Changes and acceptance

Add a short **change clause**: 'Any work or quantities beyond this scope will be quoted separately and agreed in writing before work starts.' Then make acceptance simple: a signature block with name, position, date and the words 'Accepted as written'. A WhatsApp message saying 'go ahead' is better than nothing, but a signed page is clearer if there is any disagreement later.

Writing the proposal is most of the work, but the last steps decide whether it is read at all and whether you improve over time. This lesson covers submission, follow-up and the simple tracking habits that turn each proposal into a better next one.
A person sending files
Submit early, keep proof of submission, and record every proposal you send.
Submitting correctly
Run your compliance checklist one last time against the final PDF.
Name files exactly as instructed, and check that every annex opens.
Submit at least one day before the deadline, through the channel the call specifies (portal or email).
Save proof: the portal confirmation, reference number or sent email with attachments.
Store the final version, with the call document, in your proposal folder.
Following up

For grants, wait for the funder's stated timeline. If none was given and a reasonable time has passed, a short, polite email asking whether a decision date is known is acceptable. Do not send repeated messages or try to influence reviewers. For client proposals, follow up within a few days: thank them for their time, ask if they have questions and offer a short call. Many clients simply get busy, and a polite reminder often brings a decision.

Keep your follow-up messages short and specific. For example: 'Good afternoon Ma, thank you for meeting me on Tuesday. I sent our proposal for the hostel liquid soap supply on Wednesday. Do you have any questions, or would a 10-minute call this week help? The price is valid until the 30th.' This reminds the client of the facts, invites a reply and gently points to the validity date without pressure.
Track every proposal

Keep a simple tracker in a notebook or Google Sheets with: date sent, funder or client, amount, deadline, status (submitted, shortlisted, won, lost), decision date, feedback received and lessons. Your **win rate** is proposals won divided by proposals decided, multiplied by 100.
Worked example: Amaka's first year
For example, Amaka tracks her proposals for 12 months in Google Sheets.
Grant proposals: 6 submitted, 1 won, 4 lost, 1 still waiting. Win rate = 1 won divided by 5 decided = 20%.
Client proposals: 10 sent, 6 accepted, 3 declined, 1 no response. Win rate = 6 divided by 9 decided = about 67%.
Feedback from 2 rejected grants: one said the budget lacked notes; one said the call focused on youth, which she had misread.
Lessons recorded: always write budget notes; check priorities with the go or no-go questions before writing.
Client declines: 2 of 3 said the price was high, so she now offers a smaller monthly volume as a second option.
Result: Amaka knows her strengths (client proposals) and her two fixable grant weaknesses, and her tracker guides her next applications.

Learning from rejection

Rejection is normal in proposal writing, even for experienced organisations, because most calls receive more good proposals than they can fund. If the funder offers feedback, ask for it politely and record it. Look for patterns across several rejections rather than reacting to one. Some funders welcome a revised application in a later round; check the rules before reapplying. When you do, change what the feedback pointed to, not just the date and the funder's name.

When you win a grant, your work as a writer is not finished. Read the grant agreement carefully before signing, note every reporting date and condition, and set up your project file so that receipts, attendance sheets and survey forms are collected from day one. The proposal becomes your management plan: the workplan guides your months, the budget guides your spending and the M&E plan guides your reports. Funders notice when a project is delivered exactly as proposed.
Build relationships, not just applications
Thank funders and clients whatever the result. If you win, deliver well and report on time: an organisation with a good record with one funder becomes more credible to others.

A proposal is a written offer that asks a reader to commit money to your plan. Every proposal answers one question from the reader: why should I trust you with this?

A grant proposal goes to a funder, who pays you to create change for other people. For example, Amaka in Lafia trains women to make soap and liquid detergent. She asks a foundation for about 4.8 million naira to train 40 women over 6 months.
A business proposal goes to a client who pays for her own need. In the same month, Amaka offers a school 60 litres of liquid soap per month, at an agreed price per litre.
Same skill, two very different documents, because the reader is different.
Reading the call
Five things every call tells you
Eligibility: who may apply
Funding: amounts, length, costs not allowed
Evaluation criteria and their points
Submission rules and deadline

Many proposals are rejected before anyone reads the idea, because the applicant was not eligible or ignored the format. So read the call at least three times: to understand, to mark every rule, and to check your finished draft.
First, the purpose: what change the funder wants, and who should benefit.
Second, eligibility: what type of organisation may apply, its registration, location and years of activity.
Third, funding details: the minimum and maximum amount, the project length, and costs that are not allowed.
Fourth, the evaluation criteria. Reviewers score each section, so these points tell you where to spend your effort.
And fifth, the submission rules: page limits, file type, annexes, and the exact deadline with its time zone.

Add each criterion with its points
Mark which section answers each one
Tick every row against the final document

Go through the call line by line and add every rule: eligibility, page limit, budget template, annexes, signatures and deadline.
Add every scoring criterion as its own row, with its points.
Mark which part of your proposal will answer each one.

Before you submit, tick each row against the final document, not your memory of it. Words like must and required can disqualify you. Plan to submit at least one full day early, because portals slow down near the deadline.

Writing a good proposal takes many days, so score the opportunity honestly first. Amaka finds a call for women's economic empowerment, with grants up to 5,000,000 naira for 6 to 12 months.

Her cooperative is registered, has a bank account in its own name, and has run savings groups for four years. Her plan fits the priorities and the funding range. She can meet the deadline, deliver and report.
Five yeses, so the answer is go. Design carries 30 points, so she will spend the most effort there. A clear no is also a good answer. It saves time for a better call.

Inputs: money, people, materials
Activities: what you do
Outputs: what you deliver

Funders want to see why your activities should lead to the change you promise. Inputs are your resources. Activities are what you do with them.
Outputs are what you deliver, fully under your control, like 40 women trained.
Outcomes are the change that results, like women selling and earning more. Do not put women trained at both levels.
Impact is the long-term change you contribute to. The further along the chain, the less control you have.

The executive summary is the most read part of any proposal. Some reviewers decide from it alone. It must make sense on its own, so write it last.
Amaka starts with who: her cooperative in Lafia has run savings groups for its 85 members for four years.
The problem: in her survey of 40 members, 29 earned under 20,000 naira profit a month.
What: over 6 months, train 40 women in safe soap and liquid detergent production, with starter kits, safety gear and mentoring.
Results: by month 6, at least 30 women sell regularly, and at least 25 increase monthly profit by 10,000 naira or more.
The ask: 4,815,000 naira, with storage worth 180,000 naira given by the cooperative. A reviewer knows everything in one minute.
Cover letter and checks
A one-page cover letter

The cover letter introduces your proposal on your letterhead, signed by your leader. One page: the right name and call, the project, amount and duration, why it fits, what is enclosed, and your contacts.
Then do the consistency check. List your key facts and search the document for each one. If the cover letter says 4,815,000 but the budget shows 4,850,000, reviewers start to doubt everything.
Client proposals
Vague scope or protective scope?
60 litres a month, 5-litre jerrycans
Not included: dispensers

A client does not care about your theory of change. She wants to know exactly what she will get, when, and for how much. The biggest danger is unclear scope, which leads to disputes and unpaid extra work.
Amaka's school proposal starts with the bursar's own need, then lists what is included: 60 litres a month in sealed 5-litre jerrycans, labelled, delivered on the first Monday of each month.
It also lists what is not included, such as dispensers. Exclusions feel awkward, but they protect both sides.

Keep a simple tracker of every proposal: date, funder or client, amount, status, feedback and lessons. Your win rate is proposals won, divided by proposals decided, times 100.
In her first year, Amaka sent 6 grant proposals. 1 won, 4 lost, and 1 is still waiting. 1 divided by 5 decided is 20%.
She sent 10 client proposals. 6 were accepted from 9 decided, about 67%.

Feedback showed one budget had no notes, and one call focused on youth, which she misread. Two clients said the price was high, so she now offers a smaller monthly volume as a second option. Rejection is normal. Look for patterns.
